translations.text: Then two hundred and three years had passed in the turning of the years, counted by number, and thirty [XXX] more as well, as time is reckoned, winters in the world, since the ruling God, the glory of kings, the light of the righteous, was born into this middle-earth in human form.
It was then the sixth year of Constantine's reign as emperor, since he, the war-leader, had been raised up as army-commander in the kingdom of the Romans.
The shield-protector, bold for his people, was gracious to his warriors. The prince's power grew under the heavens. He was a rightful king, a war-guardian of men.
God strengthened him with glories and with powers, so that throughout the world he became a comfort to many people and a vengeance on nations, once he raised his weapon against enemies.
Battle was offered to him, the noise of war. The people of the Huns and the Hreth-Goths gathered troops; the war-keen Franks and the Hugas marched out.

They were bold men, ready for battle. Spears gleamed, and woven mail-coats. With words and with shields they raised the war-banners. Then the hardy men were openly assembled, and the whole kin together.
The army of the peoples advanced. The wolf in the forest sang a war-song and did not hide the secret of slaughter.

The dewy-feathered eagle raised its song on the track of the enemies. Swiftly the greatest of battle-troops hastened over the city of giants, armies going to war, as many city-warriors of the neighbouring peoples as the king of the Huns could summon to battle anywhere.

The greatest of armies went forth. They drew up their foot-soldiers in mounted companies, so that the spear-brandishers in the foreign host, strong in heart, camped on the bank of the Danube, around the surging of the water.
With the uproar of their host they meant to overwhelm the kingdom of the Romans and plunder it with their armies. There the coming of the Huns became known to the city-dwellers.

Then the emperor ordered that warriors be summoned to battle with great haste, under the flight of arrows, against the fierce fighters, and that his men under the heavens be brought out to the onslaught.
The Romans, warriors famed for victory, were at once equipped with weapons for war, though they had a smaller troop for the battle than the king of the Huns;

They rode around the brave one while the shield resounded and the battle-wood clanged; the king went with his troop, with his army, to war. Above, the raven screamed, dark and fierce for slaughter. The host was on the move.
The horn-bearers leapt forward, the heralds cried out, the horse trod the earth. The army gathered, eager for strife.

The king was afraid, gripped by terror, when he saw the foreign army of the Huns and the Hreth-Goths, that it had assembled a host, a countless force, on the border of the Roman kingdom along the bank of the water.
The king of the Romans bore sorrow of heart; he had no hope for his kingdom for lack of troops. He had too few warriors, shoulder-companions, brave men for battle, against that overwhelming force.
The army encamped, the nobles around the prince, near the river, in close quarters, for the space of a night, after they had first seen the approach of the enemy.
Then, in his sleep, where he slept among his retinue, there was revealed to the emperor himself, the one renowned for victory, the call of a dream.
It seemed to him that some man appeared, beautiful in a man's form, white and bright of hue, more glorious than any he had seen before or since under the sky.
He started up from sleep, covered by the boar-banner. The messenger, the beautiful herald of glory, quickly spoke to him and called him by name (the cover of night slipped away):
"Constantine, the King of angels, the Ruler of fates, the Lord of hosts, has commanded me to offer you a covenant.
Do not be afraid, though foreigners threaten you with terror and hard battle. Look up to the heavens, to the Guardian of glory; there you will find support, a sign of victory."
At the holy one's command he was at once ready. He unlocked his heart and looked up, as the messenger, the faithful peace-weaver, had told him.
Above the roof of the clouds he saw the beautiful tree of glory, bright with ornaments and adorned with gold (gems glittered). The shining beam was inscribed with letters, bright and radiant:
"With this sign you will overcome the enemy in this perilous danger and hold back the hostile host." Then the light departed, rising upward, and the messenger with it, into the company of the pure.
Because of that fair vision, the king, lord of men, was all the happier and freer from sorrow in his heart.

Then Constantine, the protector of princes, ring-giver to warriors, war-leader of armies, the king blessed with glory, ordered in great haste that a sign, the cross of Christ, be made in the likeness of the beacon he had seen, which had earlier been shown to him in the heavens.

Then before dawn, at the break of day, he ordered the warriors to be roused and the battle-standard to be raised for the clash of weapons, and the holy tree to be carried before him into the midst of the enemies, bearing the sign of God.

Trumpets sang loudly before the armies. The raven rejoiced in the work, dewy-feathered; the eagle watched the expedition, the battle of the slaughter-fierce men. The wolf raised up a song, the dweller of the forest. The terror of battle stood ready.
There was the crash of shields and the press of men, the hard swinging of swords and the slaughter of armies, once they first met the flight of arrows.
Onto the doomed people the enemies, savagely grim, sent forth showers of arrows, spears over the yellow shields into the throng of the hostile ones, battle-adders, by the power of their fingers.

They advanced stout-hearted, pressed forward again and again, broke through the shield-covering, plunged in their blades; the ones hard in assault thronged forward. Then the banner was raised, the standard before the troops, and a victory song was sung.
Golden helmet-masks and spears gleamed on the battlefield. The heathens fell to the ground, fell without peace or protection.

The people of the Huns fled at once, as soon as the king of the Romans, the doer of battle, commanded the holy tree to be raised. The hardy warriors were scattered far and wide. War took some of them.

Some barely saved their lives in that campaign. Some fled half-alive into a stronghold and protected their lives among the stone cliffs, holding a place around the Danube. Some were carried off by drowning in the river's current at the end of their lives.
Then the brave troop was full of joy. They pursued the foreign peoples from daybreak on until evening.
Ash-wood spears flew, serpents of battle. The troop was cut down, the shield-band of the hated enemy. Only a few of the Huns' army came back home from there.
Then it was evident that the almighty King had given Constantine victory in that day's work, glorious honor, and rule under the heavens, through His rood-tree.

Then the protector of armies went back home from there, exulting in his plunder (the battle was decided), honoured by war. Then the protector of warriors came with a troop of thanes to seek his mighty dwelling; the king, brave in battle, came to visit his cities.
Then the guardian of warriors quickly commanded the wisest men to a council, those who had learned the craft of wisdom through ancient writings and held in their minds the counsels of men.

Then the leader of the people, the king victorious in battle, began to ask throughout the wide host whether there was anyone there, older or younger, who could tell him truly and make known through their lore what god this was, the giver of dwellings,
"whose sign this was that appeared to me so brightly, the brightest of tokens, and saved my people and gave me glory and success in war against my enemies through that beautiful tree."
They could not give him any answer in return, nor did they know well enough how to speak clearly about the victory-sign.
Then the wisest said in words before the army that it was the token of the King of heaven, and that there was no doubt of it.

When those who had been instructed through baptism learned that they were allowed to make known the gift of the gospel before the emperor (their minds were light and their spirits rejoiced, though they were few),
how the Protector of souls, honored in glory in the Trinity, the glory of kings, was born, and how God's own Son was hanged on the gallows before the multitudes with harsh torments.

He released the children of men, the sad spirits, from the prison of devils, and gave them grace through that same created thing that had been shown to him in a vision, the sign of victory against the attack of nations.
And how on the third day the glory of men, the Lord of all the race of men, arose from the tomb and from death, and ascended to heaven.

Thus wisely, with spiritual mysteries, they told the victorious one, as they had been taught by Sylvester. From him the leader of the people received baptism, and kept it thereafter for the time of his days, according to the Lord's will.
Then the giver of treasure, the battle-hardened king, was joyful. A new joy was placed in his heart. The guardian of the heavenly kingdom was his greatest comfort and the closest of his hopes.
Then through the gift of the Spirit he began eagerly to proclaim the law of the Lord day and night. The gold-friend of men, spear-brave and unwearying, truly devoted himself to the service of God.

Then through learned teachers the prince, protector of the people, hardened in battle and bold with the spear, found in God's books where the Ruler of the heavens had been hanged on the cross-tree amid the clamour of the crowd, out of envy, through malice,

So the old fiend led astray with lying tricks and enticed the people, the race of the Jews, so that they hanged God Himself, the Lord of hosts. For that they must endure condemnation in humiliation forever!

Then the praise of Christ was in the emperor's mind, ever mindful of the glorious tree, and he commanded his mother to travel by the land-way with a band of people to the Jews, to seek eagerly with a troop of warriors where the tree of glory, holy under the earth, was hidden, the rood of the noble King.

Helena did not wish to be slow about that journey, nor to scorn the word of the gracious giver, her own son, but she was at once ready, the woman, for the desired journey, as the protector of hosts, of mailed warriors, had commanded her.
Then a multitude of men began hastily to hurry to the ships. Sea-stallions stood ready along the ocean's shore, tethered sea-steeds, close to the water.
Then the lady's journey was well known, after she had sought out the helm of the waves with her company.

There many a proud man stood on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea. Again and again they pressed on over the border-paths, one force after another, and then they loaded the wave-stallions with battle-shirts, shields and spears, mailed warriors, men and women.
Then they let the foamy, high-prowed sea-horses glide over the ocean. Over the tossing sea, the ship's side was often struck by the blows of the waves. The sea resounded.
I never heard, before or since, of a woman leading a fairer force on the ocean stream, on the sea-road.
There one who watched that journey could see the sea-wood break over the bath-way and hasten under the swelling sails, the sea-steed play, the wave-floater wade.
The warriors were glad and bold in spirit, and the queen rejoiced in the journey, once the ring-prowed ships had crossed the expanse of water to harbour in the land of the Greeks.

At the shore they left the ships, the old wave-houses, washed by the sand and held fast by anchors, to wait on the water for the men's return, until the warrior-queen and her troop of men would come back to them over the eastern ways.

There on the warriors could plainly be seen the woven mail-coat and the tested sword, splendid war-gear, many a grim helmet, the peerless boar-standard. The spear-warriors, the men around the victory-queen, were eager for the journey.
The bold soldiers, the emperor's messengers, warriors dressed in armour, went eagerly into the land of the Greeks.
There in the war-band could be seen the set jewel, the lord's gift.

The blessed Helen was mindful, bold in thought, eager in mind to do the prince's will: that she should seek out the land of the Jews across the battlefields with a tested band of shield-warriors, a troop of men.
So it came about a short while later that the host of people, the battle-brave heroes, the spear-bold warriors, the greatest of companies, came to Jerusalem, into the city, with the noble queen.

Then she ordered that the wisest of the city-dwellers far and wide among the Jews be summoned, each of the men, to come to a council and take counsel: those who could most deeply explain the mysteries of the Lord through the true law.

Then a large company was gathered from distant ways, those who knew how to expound the law of Moses. There were three thousand of those people in number, chosen for their learning. Then the lovely woman began to address the Hebrew men with words:
"I have clearly understood, through the mysterious words of the prophets in God's books, that in days of old you were worthy in the sight of the King of glory, dear to the Lord and quick to act.
Lo, you unwisely and angrily rejected all wisdom when you cursed him who meant to release you, through the might of his glory, from damnation, from fiery torment, from captivity.

You spat filth on the face of him who brought you a remedy for the light of your eyes, renewing it from blindness through that noble spittle, and who often rescued you from the unclean spirits of devils.
You set about condemning to death him who himself raised from death people of your race, among the company of men, into their former life.
So, blind of mind, you began to mingle lie with truth, light with darkness, envy with mercy; with malicious thoughts you wove strife.
Therefore the curse harms you, guilty ones. You set about condemning the bright power, and you have lived in error, with dark thoughts, until this day.
Go now quickly, consider wisdom, men firm in wisdom, skilled in words, who hold your law, nobly skilled, foremost in your hearts,
who can truly tell me and give answer on your behalf from now on about each of the matters that I ask of them."

Then the men, faithful to the law, went off apart, sad in mind, oppressed by fear, mournful with sorrows. They eagerly sought out those wisest in mysterious words, so that they could answer the queen, whether for good or for ill, as she had asked of them.
Then they found a band of a thousand men wise in mind, who knew the ancient lore of the Jews most thoroughly.
Then they thronged in a body to where the emperor's kinswoman waited in majesty on the royal throne, the splendid war-queen adorned with gold.

Helen spoke out before the men: "Hear, wise-minded ones, a holy mystery, word and wisdom. Lo, you received the teaching of the prophets: how the Author of life, the Ruler of powers, would be born in the form of a child.

Of him Moses sang, and the guardian of Israel spoke this word: 'To you a boy shall be born in secret, glorious in powers, in such a way that his mother shall not be made pregnant with offspring through the love of a man.'

Concerning this, King David sang a lordly song, the wise prophet of old, father of Solomon, and the leader of warriors spoke this word: 'I have seen before me the God of beginnings, the Lord of victories.
He was in my sight, the Ruler of hosts, at my right hand, the Guardian of majesty. From him I shall never turn my face away, for ever.'
So again Isaiah, the prophet, deep in thought through the Spirit of the Lord, spoke in words concerning you before the hosts:
'I raised up a young offspring and begot a child, to whom I gave glory and holy comfort of mind, but they despised me and hated me in enmity; they had no forethought, no understanding of wisdom;

and the weary cattle, which people drive and thresh with every day, recognize their benefactor, and do not hate with hostile vengeance the friends who give them fodder; but the people of Israel never wanted to acknowledge me, though I performed many wonders for them through the ages of the world.'

Listen, we have heard through holy books that the Lord, the Creator, gave you unblemished glory and abundance of power, and told Moses how you should obey the King of heaven and carry out his teaching.
You soon grew weary of that, and you set yourselves against that law; you shunned the bright Creator of all, the Lord of lords, and followed error instead of God's law.
Now go quickly and find those who, through the skill of wisdom, best know the ancient writings, your law, so that they can give me an answer out of broad understanding."
Then they went with the crowd, sad in spirit, swollen with emotion, as the queen had commanded them.
Then they found five hundred very wise men, chosen from among their kinsmen, who had the most learning in their memory and wisdom in their minds.
After a little while they, the guardians of the city, were summoned again to the hall. The queen began to address them with words (she looked out over them all):
"Often you have done foolish deeds, accursed exiles, and despised the scriptures, the teaching of the fathers, but never more than now,
when you rejected the cure for blindness, and you denied truth and right: that in Bethlehem the Son of the Ruler, the only-begotten King, the chief of princes, was born.
Though you knew the law, the words of the prophets, you would not then, sinning, acknowledge the truth."

Then they answered with one mind: "Listen, we have learned the Hebrew law, which our fathers knew in former days at God's ark, and we do not clearly know why you have become so harshly angry with us, lady.
We do not know of any offence, any grievous wrong, that we have ever committed against you in this nation."
Helena made a speech and spoke before the noblemen; the lady spoke openly and aloud before the hosts:
"Now go quickly and seek out separately those among you who have the most wisdom, strength and skill of mind, so that they may boldly tell me, without hesitation, each thing that I seek from them."

Then they went from the council, as the powerful queen, bold in the cities, had commanded them. Sad at heart, they eagerly pondered and searched with careful thought what the sin might be that they had committed among the people against the emperor, for which the queen was reproaching them.
Then one man spoke there before the nobles, ready and wise in sayings, skilled in words (his name was Judas):

"I know well that she wants to inquire about the tree of victory on which the ruler of nations suffered, free of all sins, God's own Son, whom, guiltless of every crime, our fathers hanged out of hatred on the high tree in days of old.
That was a terrible thought! Now there is great need for us to make our minds firm,

so that we do not become informers about that murder, about where the holy tree was hidden after the violent assault, so that the wise ancient writings are not overthrown and the teaching of the fathers abandoned.
If this is revealed, it will not be long before the nobility of Israel, the law-skill of men, can no longer rule over the earth, just as my victorious grandfather once said long ago
(his name was Zacchaeus), the wise old prophet, to my father, his son, when he was departing from the world, and spoke these words:
'If it should happen to you in your lifetime that you hear wise men ask about the holy tree and raise disputes about the tree of victory on which the true King was hanged,
the guardian of the heavenly kingdom, the child of all peace, then make it known quickly, my dear son, before death takes you.

'Never after that can the Hebrew people, taking counsel, hold the kingdom or rule over hosts; but the glory and lordship of those who praise and laud the hanged King will live forever and ever, filled with delights.'
Then I boldly gave an answer to my father, the old man learned in the law:

'How could it ever have happened in the earthly kingdom that our fathers, in wrathful mind, laid hands on that holy one to put him to death, if they had known beforehand that he was Christ, the King in the heavens, true Son of the Creator, Saviour of souls?'
Then my elder gave me an answer; the father, wise in spirit, spoke: 'Understand, young man, the high power of God, the name of the Saviour.
It cannot be expressed by any human being; no one can trace it out by himself on this earth.
"I would never follow the counsels that this people took up. Instead I always kept myself apart from those sins and brought no shame on my soul.

I often firmly refused to take part in that wrong when the scholars of the law sat in council and considered in their minds how they might hang the Son of the Creator, the protector of men, Lord of all angels and of mankind, the noblest of children.

Yet those ill-fated men, in their folly, could not hand him over to death as they had expected, or subject him to lasting torment, even though for a while the victorious Son of God gave up his spirit on the gallows.
Afterwards, when the Ruler of the heavens, the glory of all glories, had been taken down from the cross, he remained in the tomb for three nights, under the locks of darkness,
and then on the third day the Light of all light, the Prince of angels, rose up living. The true Lord of victories, bright in glory, showed himself to his followers.
After a time your brother received the bath of baptism and the bright faith. Then, for love of the Lord, Stephen was stoned;
he did not repay evil with evil. Steadfast in his suffering, he interceded for his old enemies and begged the King of glory not to punish them for that wicked deed,
in which, through envy and at Saul's instigation, they took the life of an innocent man who was free of sin, just as Saul, out of hostility, had condemned many of Christ's people to death.
Yet the Lord afterwards showed him mercy, so that he became a comfort to many peoples. The God of beginnings, the Saviour of men, changed his name, and from then on he was called Saint Paul,

and never since has there been any better teacher of the law under the shelter of the sky, among all those whom woman or man has brought into the world, even though he had ordered Stephen, your brother, to be stoned to death on the hill.

Now you can hear, my dear man, how merciful the Ruler of all is. We often offend him and suffer the wounds of sin, but he forgives us if we soon make amends for those evil deeds and turn away from that wrong.
Therefore my dear father and I afterwards truly believed that the God of all glories, the Leader of life, suffered a terrible torment because of mankind's great need.
Therefore I teach you through this solemn counsel, dearest boy: never speak blasphemy, envy, abuse or harsh contradiction against the Son of God."
Then you will earn eternal life, the best of the rewards of victory, which will be given to you in heaven.'
This is what my father taught me in days gone by, when I was not yet grown. He instructed me with true sayings. His name was Simon, a man made wise through sorrows.
"Now you know well what you think best to reveal about this if this queen asks us about the tree, since you now know my heart and my thoughts."
Then the wisest in that crowd of men answered him: "Never in this nation have we heard any man except you, now, reveal such things about so secret an event.
You are learned in ancient songs, so do as you think best if you are questioned in the company of men.
Whoever has to answer the noble lady before such a crowd at the assembly needs wisdom, careful words and a wise man's insight."
Their speeches grew heated as the men debated on every side, some one way and some another, pondering and thinking. Then a band of thanes came to that assembly.

The heralds, the emperor's messengers, cried out: "This queen summons you men to the hall so that you may properly explain the judgments of your council. You need good counsel and wisdom of mind in the place of assembly."
They were ready, sad at heart, the protectors of the people, when they had been summoned by a stern decree; they went to the court and made known the power of their learning.

Then the queen began to address the Hebrew men, to question the weary-spirited men about the ancient scriptures: how in the world the prophets, men holy in spirit, had sung long before about the Son of God, where the Lord suffered, the true Son of the Creator, for love of souls.
They were stubborn, harder than stone. These fierce enemies would not properly reveal the mystery or give her any answer about what she was asking of them,
but they denied every word that she began to ask, firm in their minds, and said that never in their lives, before or since, had they heard anything of the kind.
Elene spoke and answered them in anger: "I will tell you truly, and it will not prove a lie while you live: if you go on any longer with this falsehood, with deceitful fraud,

…who stand before me, that fire on a hill will consume you, the hottest of fierce flames, and the leaping flame will destroy your corpses, so that this falsehood will be repaid to you with your parting from the world.
You cannot make good those words which you have for a while now wrongfully hidden under coverings of sin; you cannot hide the event or conceal the deep power."

Then they expected death, the pyre and the end of their lives, and there they handed over one man who was well versed in sayings (his name was Judas, given him by his kinsmen); they gave him to the queen and said that he was exceptionally wise:
"He can make the truth known to you and reveal the mystery of events as you question him in words, rightly from the beginning on to the end.
On earth he is of noble lineage, wise in the craft of words and a prophet's son, bold in council. It is natural to him to have wise answers and skill in his heart.
Before the multitude of men he will make known to you the gift of wisdom through the great power, as your mind desires."

She let each of them go in peace to seek his own home, and took that one man, Judas, as a hostage, and then earnestly asked him to teach the truth about the cross, which had long been hidden in its resting place, and she called him aside by himself.

Elene, the glorious queen, spoke to the solitary man: "Two things are ready for you, life or death, whichever you would rather choose. Make known quickly now what you are willing to agree to in this matter."
Judas answered her in turn (he could not escape the distress or turn aside the hostility of the king [?]; he was in the queen's power):
"How can it happen to a man who treads the moorland in the wilderness, weary and without food, held captive by hunger, when bread and stone both come into his sight together,
the hard and the soft, that he would take the stone as protection against hunger, pay no heed to the bread, turn to want and refuse the food, and scorn the better, when he has the use of both?"
Then the blessed Helena gave him an answer openly before the men:

"If you wish to have a home with the angels in the kingdom of heaven, and life on earth, and the reward of victory in the heavens, tell me quickly where the cross of the King of the heavens lies, holy beneath the ground, which you have for some time now hidden from people through the sin of murder."

Judas spoke (his mind was sad and hot at heart, and he dreaded both choices: that he should give up the hope of the heavenly kingdom and also this present realm under the heavens, and that he should not reveal the cross):
"How can I find what happened so long ago, through the passing of the years? Many have now gone by, two hundred [CC] or more counted in number.
I cannot tell it, since I do not know the number."
There are now many wise and good men, men of understanding, who were before us and have since passed away.
I was born afterwards, in later days, a young man, still a youth. I cannot find in my mind what I do not know, what happened so long ago."
Elene spoke to him in answer: "How has it come about among this people that you know in memory so fully every one of the deeds that the Trojans did in battle?
That open ancient war was much further back in the course of years than this noble event.
You can readily and quickly recount how many in all, in number of men, were slain there, spear-fighters fallen dead behind the shield-wall.
"You set down in writing the graves under the rocky slopes, and the place too, and the count of the years."
Judas spoke, bearing grievous sorrow: "We remember that warfare closely, my lady, out of necessity,
and we set down in writing the violence of battle and the conduct of the peoples; but we have never heard this made known to men from any man's mouth, except here now."

The noble queen gave him answer: "You deny too strongly the truth and what is right about the tree of life. Only a little while ago you spoke truly about the tree of victory to your people, and now you turn to a lie."
Judas answered her in turn and said that he had spoken it in distress and very much in doubt, expecting for himself a lesser affliction.
The emperor's kinswoman quickly answered him: "Listen, we have heard it made known to men through holy books that the noble son of the King was hanged on Calvary, the spiritual Son of God.
You must, in reply, reveal the knowledge, as the writings say, of where on the plain the place of Calvary is, before death takes you and you perish for your sins,

so that afterwards I may cleanse it according to Christ's will, as a help to men, so that holy God, the mighty Lord, the giver of glory to the hosts, the helper of souls, may fulfil for me the intent of my life, my desire."
Judas answered her stubbornly: "I do not know the place, and I know nothing of the plain or of the circumstances."

Helen spoke with earnest mind: "I swear by the Son of the Creator, the God who was hanged, that you shall be tormented with hunger in front of your kinsmen unless you give up these lies and tell me the truth plainly."

Then she commanded that he be led away alive by the troop, and the guilty man shoved (the servants did not delay) into a dry pit, where, without any comforts, he lingered in sorrow for the space of seven nights in that prison, tormented by hunger,
bound in fetters, and then on the seventh day, afflicted with pains, weary and without food, he began to call out (his strength was diminished):
"I beg you by the God of the heavens to let me up out of these hardships, humbled as I am by the torment of hunger.
"I will gladly make that holy tree known, now that hunger means I can hide it no longer. This captivity is so strong, the cruel need so severe, and this suffering so hard as the days go by.
I cannot endure it, nor hide any longer what I know of the tree of life, though I was once filled with folly and came to know the truth myself too late."
When she who ruled over the men there heard this, and saw how the man was behaving, she quickly ordered that he be let up out of confinement and out of the dungeon, out of that narrow house.
They carried this out at once, in haste, and led him up out of the prison with honour, as the queen had ordered them.

Then, resolute, they went to the place, up onto the hill where the Lord had once been hanged, the Guardian of the heavenly kingdom, the Son of God on the gallows. And yet he, humbled by hunger, did not know for certain

[?] where the holy cross had remained in its bed of death, shut up in the earth through the devil's cunning, held fast in its long resting place and hidden from people. At once, lacking in strength, he raised his voice and spoke in Hebrew:
"Lord Saviour, you who hold power over judgments, and who through the might of your glory made heaven and earth and the surging sea, the sea's broad expanse, and all creation together,

and you measured with your hands the whole circuit of the earth and the sky above, and you yourself sit, Ruler of victories, above the noblest race of angels, who travel through the air surrounded by light, in great majesty.
Human beings cannot travel up there from the ways of earth in the body to join that bright company, the messengers of glory. You made them and set them in your service, holy and heavenly.
Of these, six by rank are named in everlasting joy. They are surrounded and also adorned with six wings, and they shine beautifully.

Of these there are four who, always in flight, carry out their service in majesty before the face of the eternal Judge. In glory they sing the praise of the King of heaven unceasingly, with clear voices,
the most beautiful of songs, and with pure voices they speak these words (their name is cherubim): 'Holy is the holy God of the archangels, Ruler of hosts!
Heaven and earth and all the high powers are full of this glory, marked with honour.' Two among them, a victorious race in the sky, are called seraphim by name.
He must guard paradise and the holy tree of life with a flaming sword. The hard-edged blade quakes, the patterned sword trembles and changes colour, held firm in a terrible grip.
over which you, Lord God, rule forever; and you cast out of the heavens the sinful, guilt-working, reckless enemies.

Then that accursed band had to fall beneath dark dwellings into the ruin of torments, where they now suffer death-agony in the surging fire, in the dragon's embrace, wrapped in darkness. He had rejected your sovereignty.

For that he must suffer in miseries, the foulest of all foul things, guilty, and endure slavery. There he cannot throw off your word. The origin of all sin is held fast in torments, bound in hellish torment.

If it is your will, Ruler of angels, that he should reign who was on the cross, the Prince of angels who was born into the world through Mary as a child (had he not been your son, free of sin, he would never have performed so many true wonders in the earthly kingdom in the number of his days;

nor would you, Ruler of nations, have raised him from death so gloriously before the hosts, if he were not your son in glory through that bright one), then, Father of angels, send forth your sign now.
Just as you heard the holy man Moses when he spoke, when you, God of might, at that noble time revealed to the man the bones of Joseph beneath the hillside, so I [ask] you,
Joy of hosts, if it is your will, I wish to pray, through that bright creation, that you, Creator of spirits, open to me that gold-hoard which has long been hidden from people.
Now, Author of life, let a pleasant smoke rise up from that place, playing in the air, beneath the course of the sky.

I will believe the better and fix my heart more firmly, with undoubting hope, on the crucified Christ: that he is truly the Saviour of souls, eternal, almighty, King of Israel, and that he rules forever over the glory in heaven, the eternal dwellings, ever without end."
Then from that place a vapour rose up like smoke under the heavens. At this the man's heart was lifted up. Blessed and wise in the law, he clapped both hands upward.
Judas spoke, wise in thought: "Now through the truth I have come to know for myself, firmly in my heart, that you are the Saviour of the world.
Thanks be to you without end, God of hosts, enthroned in glory, that through your glory you have revealed to me, so unworthy and so sinful, the mysteries of what has happened.

Now, Son of God, gracious Giver to hosts, now that I know you are revealed and born as the majesty of all kings, I wish to ask you, Lord, to remember no more my sins, which I have committed many times.

"God of powers, let me dwell among the number of your kingdom, with the company of the saints, in that bright city where my brother Stephen is honoured in glory. He kept faith with you, though he was pelted with stones.
He has the reward for his battle, glory without end. The wonders he worked are made known in books, in writings."
Then, eager and glad and steadfast in courage, he began to dig the earth beneath the turf for the tree of glory. Twenty feet down he found it buried, hidden deep beneath the ground in a dark chamber.
There in that gloomy dwelling he found three crosses together, buried in the earth, just as a band of impious men, the race of the Jews, had covered them with earth in days of old.
They had stirred up hatred against God's Son. They would not have done so had they not listened to the teachings of the author of sins.
Then his mind was greatly gladdened, his spirit encouraged by that holy tree, and his heart inspired, once he had seen the sign lying holy beneath the earth.
He took hold of the joyful tree of glory with his hands, and with the company raised it from its grave in the earth. The travellers on foot, the nobles, went into the city.
Then the resolute, bold-hearted men set the three victory-beams in full view before Helena's knee.
The queen rejoiced in her heart at the deed, and then began to ask on which of the trees the Son of the Ruler, the giver of hope to men, had been hanged:
"Listen: we have heard through holy books, made known by signs, that two suffered with him, and he himself was the third on the cross-tree.
The whole sky grew dark in that cruel hour. Tell me, if you can, on which of these three the Lord of angels, the guardian of majesty, suffered."
Judas could not tell her clearly, nor did he fully know, which victory-beam the Saviour, God's victorious Son, had been raised up on,

until he ordered the beams to be set up with clamour in the middle of the great city, and to wait there until the almighty King revealed to them a wonder before the multitudes concerning the tree of glory.
The victorious ones sat down, deliberating together, and raised a song around the three crosses until the ninth hour. They had met with new joy through glorious deeds.

Then a crowd came there, no small company of people, and a band of men brought a dead man on a bier close by (it was then the ninth hour), a young man without breath of life. Then Judas there was greatly gladdened in his heart.

He ordered the soulless one, the body bereft of life, the lifeless man, to be set down on the earth. Then the proclaimer of right, wise in spirit and deep in thought, raised two of the crosses in his arms over that doomed house of the body.
It was as dead as before, the body held fast to its bier. The limbs grew cold, covered in dire distress. Then the third, the holy one, was raised up.
The corpse lay waiting until the Prince's cross was raised above it, the beam of heaven's King, the true sign of victory. At once he rose up, furnished again with spirit, body and soul both together.
Then praise was raised fairly among the people. They honoured the Father, and praised in words the true Son of the Ruler. To him be glory and thanks forever without end from all creation!

Then the wonders that the Lord of hosts, the guide of life, had worked to save the race of men were in the people's hearts and minds, as they always should be. Then the fiend, guilty of lies, rose up into the air, flying.
Then the devil of hell, the terrible monster, mindful of evil, began to cry out:
"What is this, oh, what man is this who again destroys my following through ancient strife, increases the old hostility, and plunders my possessions?
"This is endless strife. The souls of evildoers may no longer remain in my possession.
Now a stranger has come, whom I used to count as bound fast in sins, and he has robbed me of every right and of my treasures. That is not a fair turn of events.
The Saviour who was brought up in Nazareth has done me many harms and painful injuries. Ever since he first grew out of childhood, he has kept turning my possessions over to himself.
Now I may not rightly prosper in anything. His kingdom stretches wide over the earth, and my power under the heavens has dwindled. I have no cause to praise the cross with laughter.

Lo, the Saviour has often shut me up in the narrow home, to my sorrow in my misery! Through Judas I once became hopeful, and now I am humbled, stripped of goods, through Judas again, outlawed and friendless.

Yet afterwards I can find a way back out of the dens of the damned through accusations. I will rouse against you another king, who will persecute you, and he will abandon your teaching and follow my wicked customs,
and he will then send you into the blackest and worst terrors of torment, so that, afflicted by pains, you will firmly renounce the crucified King whom you once obeyed."

Then wise-minded Judas, the man brave in battle, answered him (the Holy Spirit had been firmly entrusted to him, fire-hot love, surging understanding through a prophet's wisdom), and spoke these words, full of wisdom:

"You need not so fiercely, mindful of sins, renew pain and stir up strife, wicked lord of murder. The mighty King, who woke many of the dead with a word, will thrust you down into the abyss, you worker of sin, into the depths of torments, stripped of glory.
Know all the more surely that in your folly you forsook the brightest of lights and the love of the Lord, that fair joy,
and ever since you have dwelt in a bath of fire, hemmed in by torments, burning on the pyre. And there forever, hostile in mind, you must endure damnation, misery without end."
Elene heard how the fiend and the friend stirred up strife on two sides, the glorious one and the wicked, the sinful and the blessed.

Her heart was the gladder because she heard that the fiend of hell, the dispenser of sins, was overcome. And then she marvelled at the man's wisdom: how he, who had been so ignorant, had in so short a time become so full of faith, steeped in wisdom.

She thanked God, the King of glory, that through the Son of God her wish had been fulfilled in both things: in the sight of the tree of victory, and in the faith that she so clearly recognized, the gift fixed in glory within the man's breast.
Then it became known in that nation, spread widely among the people, a glorious morning news, to the vexation of many of those who wished to hide the Lord's law. It was proclaimed through the towns,

in every city as far as the sea embraces, that the cross of Christ, long buried in the earth, had been found, the best of the signs of victory, of all the holy ones that were ever raised up under the heavens, early or late.
And for the Jews, those unblessed men, it was the greatest of grieving sorrows and the most hateful of fates. They would have turned aside from the world, if they could, that joy of Christians.

Then the queen commanded that messengers be sent quickly across the host of men, riding with speed. They were to seek the lord of the Romans across the deep sea and tell the warrior himself the most welcome of news:
that through the favour of the Creator the sign of victory had been met with and found in the earth, which for a long time had been hidden, to the harm of the holy ones, the Christian people.
Then the king's mind was gladdened by those glorious words, and his spirit rejoiced. There was then no lack of questioners in the towns, men in gold armour brought from far away.

At that welcome news his heart laughed, and it was the greatest comfort that had come to him in the world. The army-leaders, his messengers, brought it to him over the eastern ways: the men had made a safe journey with the victorious queen over the swan-road to the land of the Greeks.
The emperor commanded them to make themselves ready for the journey back with great haste. The men did not delay once they had quickly heard the answer, the prince's word.
He commanded that greeting be sent to Elene, brave in battle, if they had come through the sea and been allowed to make a safe journey, those bold-spirited men, to the holy city.

Constantine also commanded the messengers to tell her to build a church there on the hillside, by the counsel of them both, a temple of the Lord on Calvary, according to Christ's will, as a help to men.

There the holy cross had been found, the most glorious of trees that earth-dwellers have heard of on the earthly way. She did so, after kinsmen and friends had brought many welcome tidings from the west over the fastness of the sea.

Then the queen ordered that the best men trained in crafts be sought out separately, those who knew how to work most wondrously at joining stone, to build God's temple on that site, as the Guardian of spirits had directed her from the heavens.
Then she ordered the cross to be adorned with gold and with gems, set with skilled art with the noblest precious stones, and then locked inside a silver casket.
There the tree of life, the best of victory-trees, has remained ever since, unbroken in its nobility. There help is always ready for the sick from every torment, strife and sorrow.

There they at once find help through that holy creation, a divine grace. Judas also, after a time, received the bath of baptism, and once cleansed he became faithful to Christ and dear to the Guardian of life.
His faith became firm in his heart once the Spirit of comfort had taken up its dwelling in the man's breast and urged him to repentance.

He chose the better thing, the joy of glory, and renounced the worse, the worship of idols. He struck down false belief and unrighteous law. The eternal King, the Creator, God, Ruler of powers, became merciful to him.
Then he was baptized who for many seasons before [?] light ready [?]. His heart was inspired toward the better life and turned to glory.
Indeed, fate decreed that in this earthly kingdom he should become so faithful and so dear to God, pleasing to Christ.
This became known after Elene, on the advice of men, ordered that Eusebius, bishop of Rome, a very wise man, be brought to the holy city to give counsel and help,

so that he might ordain Judas to the priesthood in Jerusalem, as bishop for the people within the city, chosen for God's temple for his skills through the gift of the Spirit. Afterward, after wise deliberation, he gave him a new name, Cyriacus.
From then on, by the law of the Saviour, the man's name in the city was changed for the better.

Even then Elene's mind still dwelt on that glorious event, and she thought often about the nails that had pierced the Saviour's feet and his hands as well, the nails with which the Ruler of the heavens, the mighty Lord, was fastened on the cross.

The queen of the Christians began to ask about this. She asked Cyriacus to fulfil her wish once more, by the powers of the Spirit, concerning a wondrous event, and to reveal it through glorious gifts. She spoke these words to the bishop, speaking boldly:
"You, protector of men, have rightly shown me the noble tree, the cross of the King of the heavens, on which the helper of souls was hanged by heathen hands, God's own Son, the Saviour of men.
"Curiosity about the nails still urges me in my heart."
I wish that you would find those things that are still hidden in the earth, buried deep, concealed in darkness.
My mind keeps grieving and mourns in sorrow. It will not rest until the almighty Father, Lord of hosts, Saviour of men, fulfils my desire, holy from on high, through the finding of the nails.
Now, best of messengers, quickly and in all humility send your prayer into the bright creation, into the joy of glory.
Pray to the Majesty of hosts that the almighty King may reveal to you the hoard under the earth, which still lies hidden, secret from men, and waits in concealment."
Then the holy man, the bishop of the people, inspired in his breast, began to steady his mind.

Glad at heart, he went with a band of men praising God. Then Cyriacus eagerly bowed his face down on Calvary. He did not hide the secret thoughts of his heart, and by the power of the Spirit he called to God in all humility,
and prayed the Guardian of the angels to reveal to him the unknown thing, anew in his distress: where in that place he could best expect to find the nails.

Then the Father, the Spirit of comfort, sent forth a sign there where they were looking: it rose up in the colour of fire, where the noblest nails had been hidden in the earth, on the advice of men, by cruel cunning.

Then suddenly a leaping flame came, brighter than the sun. The people saw their gracious Giver make known a wonder. There, out of the darkness, the nails shone up from below out of their narrow place, lying close to the ground, and gleamed with light like the stars of heaven or golden gems.
The people rejoiced, a joyful host, and all with one mind gave glory to God, though before this they had long been in error through the devil's destruction, turned away from Christ. They spoke thus:

"Now we ourselves see the sign of victory, God's true miracle, though before we denied it with lies. Now the course of events has come into the light and been revealed. For this may the God of the kingdom of heaven have glory on high!"
Then the bishop of that people was gladdened anew, he who had turned to salvation through the Son of God.
He took up the nails, struck with awe, and brought them to the honoured queen. Cyriacus had done everything the noble woman ordered him to do, all that she wished.
Then there was a sound of weeping, and hot tears welling from her head poured down her cheeks. The tears fell over the woven wires, not at all from grief. The queen's wish was fulfilled with glory.
She knelt, bright in faith [?], and honoured the gift, exulting with joy, that had been brought to her as relief from her afflictions.
She thanked God, the Lord of victories, because she had truly come to know, here before her, what had often been proclaimed long before, from the beginning of the world, as a comfort to the peoples.
She was filled with the gift of wisdom, and the holy heavenly Spirit kept that dwelling, guarding her heart and her noble breast, and so the almighty victorious Son of God protected her afterward.

Then, through spiritual mysteries, she began to seek eagerly in her mind the way of truth to glory. Indeed the God of hosts, the Father in the heavens, the almighty King, helped her, so that the queen gained her desire in the world.
The prophecy had been sung beforehand by the sages of old, all of it from the beginning, just as it later came to pass in every matter.

Through the gift of the Spirit, the queen of the people began to inquire eagerly, closely and often, how she could best and most worthily use the nails, as a comfort to the hosts, and what the Lord's will was in this.
She then ordered that a very wise man be brought to her quickly for counsel, one wise in spirit who, through his keen ability, knew well how to give advice,
and she began to ask him what seemed best to him in his mind to do about this, and she chose to follow his teaching for the people. He boldly answered her:

"It is fitting that you keep the Lord's word, the holy mysteries, in your heart, best of queens, and eagerly carry out the King's command, now that God, the Savior of men, has given you success for your soul and the gift of wisdom.
Order these nails to be put on the bridle of the noblest of earthly kings, the rulers of cities, as bits for his horse.

This will become famous to many throughout the world, when with it he can overcome every enemy in battle, when warriors eager for war on both sides seek combat, sword-foes fighting for victory there, hostile against hostile.

Whoever leads before him that bridle on his white horse will have success in war, victory in battle, peace everywhere and safety in the fight, when battle-brave men, tested warriors, carry shield and spear into the storm of spears.

For every man, this will be an unconquered weapon in war against the monster. The prophet sang about this, a man wise in his clever thoughts (his mind went deep, the understanding of wisdom). He spoke this word:
It will come to pass, as is known, that the king's horse shall be honoured with a bit and bridle-rings under brave men.
'That sign will be called holy to God, and so will the bold and blessed one, honoured in war, whom that steed carries.'"

Then Elene quickly carried all of that out before the nobles. She ordered the prince's bridle to be adorned, the bridle of the ring-giver of men, and sent it over the ocean stream as a gift to her own son, a flawless gift.
Then she ordered the best men she knew among the Jews, of the race of heroes, to gather together and come to the holy city, into the town.
Then the queen began to teach the beloved company that they should firmly keep the love of the Lord, and likewise peace and friendship among themselves, without fault, throughout their lives,
And they obeyed the leader's teachings, the Christian customs, which Cyriacus, learned in books, commanded them. The bishopric was well established.

Often the lame, the sick in limb, the halt, the wounded and bleeding, lepers and the blind, the wretched and the sad at heart came to him from far away, believing; and there with the bishop they always found healing and remedy, everlasting for ever.
Then Elene gave him treasures as further honours, when she was eager to set out for home again; and she commanded all who praised God in that kingdom, men and women,

to honour with heart and strength, with the thoughts of their hearts, the glorious day on which the holy cross was found, the most glorious of the trees that ever grew up from the earth, sprouting under leaves.

Spring had then passed, all but six nights, before the coming of summer on the calends of May. May the door of hell be shut to every one of the people, and heaven's door opened, the eternal kingdom of the angels laid open to them, joy without end,
and their portion assigned with Mary, for whoever keeps in mind the dearest feast-day of the cross under the heavens, which the mightiest Ruler of all covered with his arms. [The end.]
Thus I, old and ready to depart because of this treacherous house, have woven with the craft of words and gathered wondrously, have pondered at times and sifted my thoughts, closely, in the night.
I did not fully know the truth about the cross until wisdom, through its glorious power, revealed a broader understanding to me in the thought of my mind.
I was stained by my deeds, fettered by sins, tormented by sorrows, bitterly bound, beset by troubles, before the mighty King granted me teaching in radiant form as a help to an old man,

measured out his flawless grace and poured it into my mind, revealed its brightness, enlarged it over time, unbound my body, unlocked my heart, released the craft of song. I have used it with joy and gladly in the world.

I often had the tree of glory in my thoughts, not just once, before I had revealed the wonder of the bright tree, as I found it made known in books, in the course of events, in writings about the sign of victory.
Until then the man had always been buffeted by surges of care, a failing ᚳ (C, cen: 'torch'), though he received treasures in the mead-hall, appled gold.

ᚣ (Y, yr: '[bow?]') lamented; the ᚾ (N, nyd: 'need') companion suffered close-pressing sorrow, a constricting secret, where before him the ᛖ (E, eoh: 'horse') measured the mile-paths, ran proudly, adorned with wire ornaments.
ᚹ (W, wynn: 'joy') is diminished, pleasure, after the years; youth has turned away, and the old pride. ᚢ (U, ur: 'our' / 'aurochs') was once the radiance of youth.

Now the days of old have departed after their appointed span, the joys of life have slipped away, as ᛚ (L, lagu: 'water') glides away, the driven floods. ᚠ (F, feoh: 'wealth') is fleeting for everyone under the sky;

the ornaments of the land pass away under the clouds most like the wind, when it rises loud before men, roams by the clouds, travels raging, and then suddenly grows silent again, closely confined in its prison, crushed down by force.
So this whole world will pass away, and likewise those who were brought forth in it will be seized by the flame of torment, when the Lord himself comes to judgement with a host of angels.

There every one of those endowed with speech shall hear the true verdict on each of their deeds through the mouth of the Judge, and likewise give pledge for their words, for all the folly spoken before, the reckless thoughts.
Then he will divide into three parts, in the grip of the fire, every single one of the people who have lived throughout the ages across the wide earth.
The righteous will be uppermost in that fire, the company of the blessed, the host eager for glory, so that they can endure it and bear it easily without hardship, the host of the brave-hearted.

For them the whole light of the fire will be tempered, as is easiest for them and most comfortable to themselves. The sinful will be tormented in the middle, stained with crimes, sad-hearted men in the hot surge, covered over with smoke.

The third part, the accursed evil-doers, will be at the bottom of the surge: false enemies of the people, held fast in the flame because of their former deeds, the throng of the wicked, in the grip of the burning coals.

Never afterwards will they come from that house of torment into the remembrance of God, the King of glory. Instead they will be thrown from that fierce surge into the depths of hell, those hostile enemies. It will be different for the other two parts.

They will be allowed to see the Lord of angels, the God of victories. They will be refined and separated from sins, like pure gold that is entirely cleansed of every stain in the surge of the furnace's fire, purified and melted.
In the same way each of those people will be cut away and separated from every guilt and from deep crimes through the fire of judgment.

Then afterwards they will be allowed to enjoy peace and eternal happiness. The Guardian of angels will be gentle and kind to them, because they rejected every crime and the work of sins, and called out with words to the Son of the Creator.
Therefore they now shine in beauty like the angels, and enjoy the inheritance of the King of glory forever. Amen.
